lead: A security course needs three words kept apart. An attack is an action that breaks something. A service is a promise the system makes to its users, such as "nobody else can read this". A mechanism is the tool that keeps that promise, such as encryption. The service and mechanism lists come from X.800, an ITU-T standard. The four attack classes come from the OSI attack taxonomy used in the standard security texts. Exam questions ask you to move between the three columns.
prereq: You need 1.1, because each service here protects one of the three goals defined there.

blocks.text: Watch one message travel from sender to receiver and ask what an attacker can do. There are four answers.

items: Interruption: the message or the service is destroyed or blocked. Goal: availability.
Interception: an unauthorised party reads the message. Goal: confidentiality.
Modification: the message is changed before it arrives. Goal: integrity.
Fabrication: a new message is inserted and made to look like it came from a real sender. Goals: integrity and authentication.

blocks.text: These four are the attack classes. Every named attack is one of them. A man-in-the-middle attack is interception plus modification. A flood that drowns a server is interruption.

A second cut is passive and active. A passive attack only observes. Two forms: release of message contents, and traffic analysis, which reads who talks to whom, when, and how many bytes, even when the bytes are scrambled. Nothing changes, so no checksum fails and detection is almost impossible. Defence is prevention: encryption, traffic padding, careful routing.

An active attack changes the data stream or the service: interruption, modification, fabrication, masquerade, replay. Something now looks wrong, so the aim is detection plus recovery. Only interception is purely passive; the other three classes are active.

Where does replay sit? The copying is passive interception; the re-insertion is active. Its class is contested. Most texts call it modification of the message stream, because an old message is put in place of the fresh one expected. Some list it as fabrication, because a copy is inserted. Either answer is accepted; say which you mean.
A security service is a guarantee the system gives its users. The standard list has six items, from X.800. A service says what is promised, never how it is done.

items: Authentication: peer entity authentication proves who the other side is at the start of a connection. Data origin authentication proves which party created one message, with or without a connection.
Access control: only the listed users, under the listed conditions, may use a resource.
Data confidentiality: content is unreadable to others. Four forms: connection, connectionless, selective field, and traffic flow (the pattern and volume are hidden too).
Data integrity: the data arrives exactly as sent, with no change, insertion, deletion or replay.
Non-repudiation: a party cannot later deny a message. Two forms: proof of origin, and proof of delivery.

blocks.text: Two pairs are easy to confuse. Integrity is not confidentiality: a readable message can still be protected against tampering, and an unreadable one can still be tampered with. Non-repudiation is not authentication: authentication convinces the receiver at the time, while non-repudiation convinces a third party, such as a court, months later.
A mechanism is the tool or procedure that delivers a service. The standard list has eight. Some syllabi call mechanisms security controls and split them into preventive, detective and corrective.

items: Encipherment: turning plaintext into ciphertext. Delivers confidentiality, and supports integrity and authentication when a key is involved.
Digital signature: data plus a private-key transformation that anyone can check. Delivers integrity, origin authentication and non-repudiation.
Access control mechanisms: passwords, access lists, capabilities, roles.
Data integrity mechanisms: a check value or sequence number attached to the data, so any change is visible.
Authentication exchange: a message protocol, such as challenge and response, that tests a claim of identity.
Traffic padding: extra bits or extra messages, so the real length and timing are hidden.
Routing control: choosing trusted links and relays, or changing route when one is suspect.
Notarization: a trusted third party records facts about a message, such as time, origin and delivery.

blocks.text: The mapping is many-to-many. Non-repudiation needs a signature plus a timestamp from a notary. One signature gives integrity, origin authentication and non-repudiation in one action.

spec.aria: A four-column grid of chips: event, attack class, service and mechanism, for packet copying, the changed amount, the 3-hour outage and the denied sending.

examples.question: An employee downloads the salary file from the office server. For each event give the attack class (if any), the service attacked, and one mechanism that would have helped. Compute the change in rupees and the outage in minutes and seconds. (a) A switch mirror copies the packets, but the file body is unreadable. (b) The amount field changes in transit from ₹45,000 to ₹95,000. (c) The file server stops answering for 3 hours. (d) After the transfer the sender denies sending the file.
steps: (a) The attacker only copies; nothing is altered. Attack class = interception, passive. The contents stayed safe because encipherment was already applied. What is still exposed is the pattern of who sent what to whom and when; traffic padding and careful routing reduce that.
(b) The value inside the message changed. Attack class = modification, active. Service attacked = data integrity. Mechanism = a MAC or a digital signature over the amount field.
(c) The service stopped. Attack class = interruption, active. Service attacked = availability. Mechanism = redundancy, plus rate limiting at the edge. No cipher helps here.

(d) The message was genuine, but the sender now refuses to admit it. This is not one of the four message classes; it is the X.800 threat of repudiation. The receiver cannot later prove the sender sent the file, so the missing service is non-repudiation, met by a digital signature with a notarised timestamp. If a class must be named, note only that a false denial by a party is treated as fabrication by the receiving side.
Arithmetic for the outage: 3 hours × 60 = 180 minutes; 180 × 60 = 10,800 seconds.
examples.answer: The amount changed by ₹50,000 and the outage lasted 180 minutes (10,800 seconds). The events map to interception (encipherment already protected the contents), modification (MAC or signature), interruption (redundancy), and repudiation (non-repudiation service, digital signature with notarised timestamp).

old = 45000

delta = new - old
hours = 3

traps: Mixing the three columns. Writing "encryption" when a service is asked for, or "confidentiality" when a mechanism is asked for, loses marks. Read what the question wants: what breaks, what is promised, or how it is done.
Calling a replay passive. The copying is passive interception, but the re-insertion is active. Say "modification of the message stream, sometimes listed as fabrication".
Treating authentication and non-repudiation as one service. Authentication convinces the receiver at the time; non-repudiation must convince a third party later.
Assuming encryption covers all of confidentiality. Traffic analysis still works on an encrypted stream, so traffic-flow confidentiality needs padding and routing control as well.
Writing "encryption" as the mechanism against a DoS attack. Availability is met by redundancy, rate limiting and routing control, not by secrecy.

quiz.q: Name the four attack classes and the goal each one attacks.
quiz.a: Interruption attacks availability, interception attacks confidentiality, modification attacks integrity, fabrication attacks integrity and authentication.
Authentication, access control, data confidentiality, data integrity, non-repudiation, availability.

quiz.q: Why is a passive attack hard to detect, and what does that mean for defence?
quiz.a: Nothing is altered, so no check fails and no trace is left in the data. Defence is prevention: encryption, traffic padding, routing control, rather than detection after the fact.

quiz.q: State the difference between peer entity authentication and data origin authentication.
quiz.a: Peer entity authentication runs at connection setup and proves who is at the other end for the life of the connection. Data origin authentication proves the source of a single message, works without a connection, and says nothing about timing or other messages.

quiz.q: A captured message "PAY ₹45,000" is re-sent three times next week. Classify the attack, name the service broken, and give two mechanisms that would stop it.
quiz.a: Active attack. Its class is contested: modification of the message stream, sometimes listed as fabrication (replay); either is accepted. Services broken: data integrity, and also authentication and non-repudiation. Mechanisms: a data integrity mechanism with timestamps or sequence numbers that rejects old messages, and a digital signature so the copy cannot pass as fresh.

quiz.q: A switch mirror copies an encrypted stream. The payload is safe, but the attacker still learns which client talks to the server and for how long. Name the attack sub-type, the service that is missing, and one mechanism for it.
quiz.a: Passive interception of the traffic pattern, i.e. traffic analysis. Service missing: traffic-flow confidentiality. Mechanism: traffic padding, with routing control as a second option.

quiz.q: It is claimed that one digital signature gives three services at once. Which three, and where does the mechanism fail?
quiz.a: Data integrity (any change breaks the check), data origin authentication (only the private-key holder can produce it), and non-repudiation (the holder cannot deny it). It gives no confidentiality, because anyone with the public key reads the message. It gives no availability, because an attacker can still block delivery. It also fails if the private key is stolen, since the thief can sign in the owner's name.

beyond: Not for the exam. X.800 survives because auditors need a fixed checklist: a security architecture document is a table of services, the mechanism that delivers each, and the person who owns it. Modern threat modelling frameworks such as STRIDE are close cousins, with one letter for each of spoofing, tampering, repudiation, information disclosure, denial of service and elevation of privilege. Zero-trust designs keep the same services but move the mechanisms from the network edge to every request.
